Most soft-bristle brushes, and brushes with end-rounded tips, tended to remove plaque and ease gingivitis better. In the studies, the Bass method had a positive effect when used twice a day for at least two minutes.

### What it means for you
The ideal time to replace a brush cannot be confirmed yet: the authors say well-designed trials are needed. The overall findings can still guide daily brushing. Your dentist or hygienist can show you the technique.

Plain-language retelling of a published paper. Original:
- Kaneyasu Y, Shigeishi H, Niitani Y, Takemoto T, Sugiyama M, Ohta K. Manual toothbrushes, self-toothbrushing, and replacement duration to remove dental plaque and improve gingival health: A scoping review from recent research. J Dent. 2024. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jdent.2024.105240 https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/39038528/

## Sensitivity toothpaste after whitening
URL: https://saysmiledent.github.io/SaySmile/en/articles/sensitivity-toothpaste-after-whitening/
Published: 2026-11-01

A systematic review of 5 studies (387 people): desensitising toothpastes helped after some whitening protocols and did not help after others.

- A systematic review of 5 studies with 387 people.
- Desensitising toothpaste helped after at-home bleaching with 22% carbamide peroxide and one in-office session with 35% hydrogen peroxide.
- It did not help with the other bleaching regimens.

### What was studied
Teeth often become sensitive after bleaching. The authors checked whether desensitising toothpaste helps in that case. The review included 5 randomised trials with 387 people.

### What was found
The toothpaste worked after at-home bleaching with 22% carbamide peroxide and after a single in-office session with 35% hydrogen peroxide. It was not effective for at-home bleaching with 16% carbamide peroxide or for two in-office sessions with 35% or 38% hydrogen peroxide.

### What it means for you
The authors conclude that the result depends on the bleaching regimen and more research is needed. If your teeth react to cold after whitening, tell the dentist who did it.

Plain-language retelling of a published paper. Original:
- Cabral AEA, Lourenço MAG, de Medeiros Santos BS, Carvalho MG, Pazinatto RB, Leite FPP, et al.. Effectiveness of desensitizing toothpastes in reducing tooth sensitivity after tooth bleaching: a systematic review. Clin Oral Investig. 2024. https://doi.org/10.1007/s00784-024-05857-2 https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/39078468/

## Sensitive teeth in children with MIH
URL: https://saysmiledent.github.io/SaySmile/en/articles/sensitive-teeth-in-children-with-mih/
Published: 2026-11-01

In children with molar-incisor hypomineralisation, sealing helped mild cases and crowns helped severe ones. The studies were small.

- MIH (molar-incisor hypomineralisation) can make a child's teeth very sensitive.
- Sealing with resin or glass ionomer helped most in mild cases, crowns in severe ones.
- Conclusions are limited: few participants and short follow-up.

### What was studied
MIH is a defect in the enamel of the first permanent molars and incisors that can make teeth very sensitive to cold, heat and brushing. The authors examined which treatments reduce this sensitivity in children aged 6 to 18.

### What was found
Eight papers were included, six of them pooled in a meta-analysis. Different methods helped: desensitising mousse, sealing, laser therapy and crowns, each significantly reducing sensitivity.

### What it means for you
The best reduction came from sealing with composite or glass ionomer for mild MIH and from crowns for severe MIH. But the number of participants was small and follow-up short, which limits the conclusions. If a child's teeth react painfully to cold, show them to a children's dentist.

Plain-language retelling of a published paper. Original:
- Hjertberg E, Hajdarević A, Jälevik B. Desensitization treatment in MIH-affected teeth: a systematic review. Eur Arch Paediatr Dent. 2024. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40368-024-00934-2 https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/39136874/

## Bite changes and jaw pain (TMD)
URL: https://saysmiledent.github.io/SaySmile/en/articles/bite-changes-and-jaw-pain-tmd/
Published: 2026-11-01

Cochrane: across 57 studies our confidence in the benefit of splints and bite adjustments is low. Larger, better trials are needed.

- Cochrane: 57 studies, 2,846 participants with temporomandibular disorders (TMD).
- Occlusal splints were compared with no treatment, placebo and other treatments.
- Results are inconclusive; certainty is very low.

### What was studied
Temporomandibular disorders cause pain in the jaw muscles or joint and other problems. Occlusal splints (dental guards) are often used. Cochrane assessed 57 studies with 2,846 participants comparing splints with no treatment, placebo or another treatment. Most evaluated the full hard stabilisation splint. Only one study was at low risk of bias.

### What was found
This splint may reduce muscle pain when chewing compared with no treatment, and orofacial myofunctional therapy may reduce joint noise more than the splint, but in both cases the evidence is very uncertain. For all other comparisons and outcomes there may be little or no difference, and again the evidence is very uncertain.

### What it means for you
The authors conclude the results are inconclusive and the research questions remain unanswered. If your jaw hurts or clicks, do not pick a treatment yourself: diagnosis and the plan are for your dentist.

Plain-language retelling of a published paper. Original:
- Singh BP, Singh N, Jayaraman S, Kirubakaran R, Joseph S, Muthu MS, et al.. Occlusal interventions for managing temporomandibular disorders. Cochrane Database Syst Rev. 2024. https://doi.org/10.1002/14651858.CD012850.pub2 https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/39282765/

## Gum treatment in pregnancy
URL: https://saysmiledent.github.io/SaySmile/en/articles/gum-treatment-in-pregnancy/
Published: 2026-11-01

Certain periodontal treatments may lower the risk of preterm birth and low birth weight.

- A network meta-analysis of 20 randomised trials in pregnant women.
- Three gum treatment strategies reduced the risk of preterm birth.
- Two reduced the risk of preterm birth and/or low birth weight.

### What was studied
Gum disease is widespread among pregnant women, and improving oral health may improve pregnancy outcomes. Using a network meta-analysis, the authors compared different periodontal treatment strategies. It covered 20 randomised trials and 5 outcomes: preterm birth, low birth weight, the two combined, small for gestational age and pre-eclampsia.

### What was found
Three strategies reduced the risk of preterm birth: scaling and root planing with chlorhexidine rinsing; that plus tooth polishing and plaque control; and scaling and root planing with a sonic toothbrush, polishing and plaque control. The first two also reduced the risk of preterm birth and/or low birth weight.

### What it means for you
The authors conclude that certain gum treatments can lower these risks, and future studies should refine the strategies and the best timing in different periods of pregnancy. If you are pregnant, see a dentist; it is best to plan gum treatment together with your obstetrician.

Plain-language retelling of a published paper. Original:
- Wu J, Wu J, Tang B, Zhang Z, Wei F, Yu D, et al.. Effects of different periodontal interventions on the risk of adverse pregnancy outcomes in pregnant women: a systematic review and network meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials. Front Public Health. 2024. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpubh.2024.1373691 https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/39371200/

## Probiotics in gum treatment
URL: https://saysmiledent.github.io/SaySmile/en/articles/probiotics-in-gum-treatment/
Published: 2026-11-01

A network meta-analysis of 33 articles (1,290 patients): probiotics added to professional cleaning may improve gum condition, with Lactobacillus showing the strongest effects.

- A network meta-analysis of 33 articles with 1,290 patients.
- Probiotics added to professional cleaning may improve pocket depth and gum attachment further.
- Lactobacillus showed the strongest effects.

### What was studied
Probiotics are helpful microorganisms. The authors checked whether they help in non-surgical gum treatment, when the dentist removes plaque and tartar from the pockets. Professional cleaning combined with probiotics was compared with professional cleaning plus a placebo.

### What was found
The analysis covered 33 articles and 1,290 patients. The main outcomes were pocket depth and attachment level, with bleeding, plaque and bacterial colony counts as secondary outcomes. Results were split by follow-up time and by duration of probiotic use. Significant differences were found in pocket depth for nine probiotic interventions, in attachment for eighteen and in bleeding for eight.

### What it means for you
The conclusion: cleaning together with probiotics may be more effective in improving pocket depth and attachment, with Lactobacillus the most effective. A probiotic does not replace cleaning, and the decision about it is the dentist's.

Plain-language retelling of a published paper. Original:
- Mendonça CD, Mata ADSPD, Azevedo LFR, Marques JF, Silveira JML, Marques DNDS. Probiotics in the non-surgical treatment of periodontitis: a systematic review and network meta-analysis. BMC Oral Health. 2024. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12903-024-05027-6 https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/39407177/

## Silver diamine fluoride (SDF) for decay
URL: https://saysmiledent.github.io/SaySmile/en/articles/silver-diamine-fluoride-sdf-for-decay/
Published: 2026-11-01

SDF is used to stop decay in children and older adults. The evidence is low in certainty, and tooth staining was poorly reported.

- SDF (silver diamine fluoride) is a liquid painted onto decayed spots to stop decay.
- In children it may help stop decay that has started; on roots of older adults it probably prevents new decay.
- Staining of teeth was poorly reported, and certainty is low for many outcomes.

### What was studied
SDF is a liquid applied to a decayed spot to halt the process without drilling. Cochrane pooled 29 trials with 13,036 participants, of whom 12,020 were children and 1,016 older adults. SDF was compared with placebo, no treatment and fluoride varnish.

### What was found
In baby teeth, evidence on preventing new decay is uncertain, but SDF may help arrest decay that has already started. On tooth roots in adults it probably helps prevent new decay. Compared with fluoride varnish in baby teeth it adds little, though certainty is low.

### What it means for you
Staining (silver darkens the treated spot) was poorly reported, and evidence on side effects is very uncertain. Whether SDF fits your case is for your dentist to decide; the authors ask for new, better-run studies.

Plain-language retelling of a published paper. Original:
- Worthington HV, Lewis SR, Glenny AM, Huang SS, Innes NP, O'Malley L, et al.. Topical silver diamine fluoride (SDF) for preventing and managing dental caries in children and adults. Cochrane Database Syst Rev. 2024. https://doi.org/10.1002/14651858.CD012718.pub2 https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/39508296/

## Gentle care for sensitivity in MIH
URL: https://saysmiledent.github.io/SaySmile/en/articles/gentle-care-for-sensitivity-in-mih/
Published: 2026-11-01

A meta-analysis of 15 studies in children: CPP-ACP reduced sensitivity more than fluoride varnish, but the evidence is mixed and limited.

- A meta-analysis of 15 studies in children with molar incisor hypomineralisation (MIH).
- CPP-ACP was no better than fluoride at strengthening enamel.
- It reduced sensitivity more than fluoride varnish in some studies, but the results were inconsistent.

### What was studied
MIH is a condition where the enamel of the first permanent molars (and sometimes the incisors) is weak and patchy. These teeth are often sensitive. The authors gathered data on gentle care for such teeth in children under 18. They found 1,566 studies and 15 entered the meta-analysis.

### What was found
CPP-ACP showed no significant advantage over fluoride for remineralisation. For reducing sensitivity it did better than fluoride varnish (mean difference -2.36), but the results were highly inconsistent (I² 83%). Calcium glycerophosphate and silver diamine fluoride showed mild benefits.

### What it means for you
The conclusion: there is not yet solid evidence that any one product is clearly better. A child with sensitive, weak teeth needs an examination, and the dentist chooses the method.

Plain-language retelling of a published paper. Original:
- Cavalcante BGN, Mlinkó É, Szabó B, Teutsch B, Hegyi P, Vág J, et al.. Non-Invasive Strategies for Remineralization and Hypersensitivity Management in Molar-Incisor Hypomineralization-A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis. J Clin Med. 2024. https://doi.org/10.3390/jcm13237154 https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/39685613/

## How common is gum disease
URL: https://saysmiledent.github.io/SaySmile/en/articles/how-common-is-gum-disease/
Published: 2026-11-01

A meta-analysis of 55 studies from 2011 to 2020 put periodontitis at about 62% of adults who still have their teeth, and severe periodontitis at 23.6%.

- A meta-analysis of 55 studies from 2011 to 2020.
- Gum disease in adults who still have their teeth was estimated at about 62%, severe disease at 23.6%.
- Among people aged 65 and over the estimate reached 79.3%.

### What was studied
Periodontitis is inflammation of the tissues around the teeth and can lead to tooth loss. The authors asked how common it is in people who still have their teeth. The analysis covered 55 studies from 2011 to 2020, from 17 countries.

### What was found
The result depended on how the disease was defined. With confident case definitions 61.6% had periodontitis, with less strict ones 38.5%. Among the CDC/AAP definitions the 2012 version gave the highest estimate (68.1%) and the 2007 version the lowest (48.8%). The older the group, the higher the share: for people aged 65 and over it was 79.3%.

### What it means for you
The authors conclude that between 2011 and 2020 periodontitis in adults with teeth was around 62% and severe periodontitis 23.6%, which is high compared with earlier estimates from 1990 to 2010. If your gums bleed or a tooth feels loose, do not put off a check-up.

Plain-language retelling of a published paper. Original:
- Trindade D, Carvalho R, Machado V, Chambrone L, Mendes JJ, Botelho J. Prevalence of periodontitis in dentate people between 2011 and 2020: A systematic review and meta-analysis of epidemiological studies. J Clin Periodontol. 2023. https://doi.org/10.1111/jcpe.13769 https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36631982/

## Building better brushing habits
URL: https://saysmiledent.github.io/SaySmile/en/articles/building-better-brushing-habits/
Published: 2026-11-01

A review of behaviour-change approaches that help people keep up oral hygiene and gum health. Their clinical effect still needs more research.

- Gum disease affects half of the world's population, and plaque control has to be steady.
- Approaches that work on beliefs, motivation and self-control may improve gum health.
- The approaches cannot be compared directly, and more clinical studies are needed.

### What was studied
Gum health depends on how a person cleans their teeth every day. So dentists increasingly use psychological models to understand the patient and support self-care. The authors described these models and the results of programmes built on them.

### What was found
The models describe how a person becomes aware of a problem, decides to change, plans it and keeps track. A newer system, COM-B, is used more and more in dental settings. Within the limits of the evidence, approaches that address beliefs, motivation, intention and self-regulation may improve gum health.

### What it means for you
The approaches cannot be compared head to head because protocols, groups and follow-up times differ too much. The practical takeaway: knowing you should brush is not enough, and a clear plan with support helps. If a habit is hard to keep, tell your dentist, who can suggest ways.

Plain-language retelling of a published paper. Original:
- Chan CCK, Chan AKY, Chu CH, Tsang YC. Theory-based behavioral change interventions to improve periodontal health. Front Oral Health. 2023. https://doi.org/10.3389/froh.2023.1067092 https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36762002/

## Probiotics for oral health
URL: https://saysmiledent.github.io/SaySmile/en/articles/probiotics-for-oral-health/
Published: 2026-11-01

A review of how probiotics and postbiotics may affect decay, thrush, gum disease and bad breath.

- Probiotics and postbiotics are being studied for decay, thrush, gum disease and bad breath.
- The idea: helpful bacteria reduce harmful ones, as happens in the gut.
- This is a review of research, not advice on what to buy.

### What was studied
Oral diseases affect most people at some point in life. Decay depends on the mix of microbes in the mouth, and one of them is seen as the main culprit. So researchers test whether probiotics, which help the gut, might help in the mouth too.

### What was found
The authors looked at how different probiotic strains affect decay, yeast infections, gum disease and bad breath. They also discuss postbiotics: non-living compounds derived from probiotics.

### What it means for you
This is an active area, but the review gives no ready recommendations. Probiotic products do not replace brushing and treatment. If you want to try one, ask your dentist which strains have actually been studied.

Plain-language retelling of a published paper. Original:
- Homayouni Rad A, Pourjafar H, Mirzakhani E. A comprehensive review of the application of probiotics and postbiotics in oral health. Front Cell Infect Microbiol. 2023. https://doi.org/10.3389/fcimb.2023.1120995 https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36968114/

## Laser for tooth sensitivity
URL: https://saysmiledent.github.io/SaySmile/en/articles/laser-for-tooth-sensitivity/
Published: 2026-11-01

A systematic review of 34 studies: lasers of either power reduced pain after 3 months, though no single protocol has been established.

- A systematic review of laser treatment for dentin sensitivity: 34 studies.
- Both high- and low-power lasers reduced pain at 3 months.
- There is no single protocol yet: the methods differ widely between studies.

### What was studied
A laser is sometimes used to ease the sharp tooth pain caused by cold and sweet foods. The authors checked how well it works. They included 34 studies, 11 of which entered the meta-analysis.

### What was found
High- and low-power lasers both reduced pain at 3 months. High-power lasers tended to reduce it more, but the difference was not significant. There is no defined protocol because the studies used different methods and settings. About 55% followed patients for 6 months at most.

### What it means for you
The conclusion: a laser can be a treatment option, but longer and more uniform studies are needed. Whether it suits you is decided by your dentist after an examination.

Plain-language retelling of a published paper. Original:
- Pion LA, Matos LLM, Gimenez T, Palma-Dibb RG, Faraoni JJ. Treatment outcome for dentin hypersensitivity with laser therapy: Systematic review and meta-analysis. Dent Med Probl. 2023. https://doi.org/10.17219/dmp/151482 https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/37023343/

## Retainers after braces
URL: https://saysmiledent.github.io/SaySmile/en/articles/retainers-after-braces/
Published: 2026-11-01

Cochrane: 47 studies, 4,377 participants; low-certainty evidence does not let us name the best type of retainer.

- Cochrane 2023: 47 studies, 4,377 participants.
- Certainty of the evidence is low or very low; 28 studies had a high risk of bias.
- There are no firm conclusions about which retainer is best.

### What was studied
After braces come off, teeth can drift back, so retainers are fitted. Cochrane compared retainer types for stability, comfort and gum health. It included 47 studies and 4,377 participants; 28 of them had a high risk of bias.

### What was found
Part-time clear plastic lower retainers had slightly more relapse than fixed ones, but not by a clinically important amount; they caused more discomfort, failed less and gave healthier gums. Full-time clear plastic retainers gave no clinically significant benefit for stability, with less gum bleeding and more failures. Clear plastic and Hawley retainers had similar stability: Hawley retainers fail less but are less comfortable.

### What it means for you
The authors conclude that the certainty is low, so no firm conclusions can be drawn. The choice of retainer and how long to wear it is up to your orthodontist.

Plain-language retelling of a published paper. Original:
- Martin C, Littlewood SJ, Millett DT, Doubleday B, Bearn D, Worthington HV, et al.. Retention procedures for stabilising tooth position after treatment with orthodontic braces. Cochrane Database Syst Rev. 2023. https://doi.org/10.1002/14651858.CD002283.pub5 https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/37219527/

## Second-hand smoke and children's teeth
URL: https://saysmiledent.github.io/SaySmile/en/articles/second-hand-smoke-and-children-s-teeth/
Published: 2026-11-01

The review found a significant link between passive smoking and decay in baby teeth. Parents should know about it.

- A review of 25 studies: second-hand smoke is linked to more decay in baby teeth.
- In 94% of studies a link was found; three showed a dose-response pattern.
- Smoke exposure during pregnancy was linked to decay more strongly than exposure after birth.

### What was studied
Passive smoking means breathing other people's tobacco smoke. The authors checked how it affects the teeth of infants, preschoolers and children. From 1,221 records, 25 studies remained after screening.

### What was found
In 94.4% of studies a link was found between passive smoking and higher decay prevalence, and three suggested a dose-response relationship. In 81.8% of studies exposure before birth was linked to more decay than exposure after birth. Low parental education, socioeconomic status, diet, hygiene and gender affected how much smoke children were exposed to.

### What it means for you
The authors see passive smoking as a risk factor for oral health, both before and after birth. Clinicians should ask about it when taking a child's history, and parents should know how smoke affects a child's teeth and general health.

Plain-language retelling of a published paper. Original:
- Uthayakumar T, Bennett JX, Cartas HL, Brunet M, Vo KL, Kroon J. Passive Smoking and Oral Health of Infants, Preschoolers, and Children: A Systematic Review. Nicotine Tob Res. 2023. https://doi.org/10.1093/ntr/ntad093 https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/37311007/

## Wear notches at the tooth neck
URL: https://saysmiledent.github.io/SaySmile/en/articles/wear-notches-at-the-tooth-neck/
Published: 2026-11-01

Composite with adhesive worked well for restoring wear lesions at the tooth neck. A diode laser may reduce sensitivity.

- Composite with an adhesive restores wear notches at the tooth neck well.
- A diode laser before filling does not reduce how well the filling stays and may lessen sensitivity.
- The review rests on 11 clinical studies.

### What was studied
Non-carious cervical lesions are areas of enamel and dentine lost near the gum line through wear, not decay. The enamel there is thin and bonding to dentine is weaker. The authors asked how best to restore such lesions with little intervention and whether a diode laser can reduce sensitivity.

### What was found
They searched three databases for work from 2018 to 2023 and selected 11 clinical and randomised trials. Composite resins performed well in restoring these lesions.

### What it means for you
Composite placed after an adhesive proved efficient and effective. Using a diode laser before filling did not reduce how long fillings stayed in place, may lessen hypersensitivity and may affect treatment success. If you notice sensitive notches near the gum line, show your dentist: they will find the cause and choose a method.

Plain-language retelling of a published paper. Original:
- Patano A, Malcangi G, De Santis M, Morolla R, Settanni V, Piras F, et al.. Conservative Treatment of Dental Non-Carious Cervical Lesions: A Scoping Review. Biomedicines. 2023. https://doi.org/10.3390/biomedicines11061530 https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/37371625/

## Bad breath: causes and care
URL: https://saysmiledent.github.io/SaySmile/en/articles/bad-breath-causes-and-care/
Published: 2026-11-01

A review of what causes bad breath and how it is diagnosed and managed. It can sometimes signal an underlying illness.

- Bad breath gets in the way of social life and daily routine.
- It can sometimes be a sign of another illness.
- To treat it properly, the cause has to be found first.

### What was studied
Halitosis is an unpleasant odour in exhaled air, whatever its cause. Most people who have it feel embarrassed, and it affects how they get on with others. The authors described the causes and how patients are managed, because GPs and dentists need to know them.

### What was found
Knowing the causes helps in making an accurate diagnosis and choosing prevention and treatment. The authors also stress that bad breath can be a sign of an underlying disease, so the problem should not be pushed aside.

### What it means for you
If breath odour worries you, do not be shy about asking: a clinician can find the cause and suggest prevention. This is a reference for professionals rather than a ready-made recipe, so it is best not to guess at home remedies without knowing the cause.

Plain-language retelling of a published paper. Original:
- Khounganian RM, Alasmari ON, Aldosari MM, Alghanemi NM. Causes and Management of Halitosis: A Narrative Review. Cureus. 2023. https://doi.org/10.7759/cureus.43742 https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/37727189/

## Sealants for baby teeth
URL: https://saysmiledent.github.io/SaySmile/en/articles/sealants-for-baby-teeth/
Published: 2026-11-01

Cochrane found little evidence on sealants for baby teeth (9 studies, 1,120 children), and side effects were rarely reported.

- Cochrane found only 9 studies of sealants for baby teeth, 1,120 children.
- Certainty of evidence is low or very low.
- Side effects were rarely reported.

### What was studied
A sealant covers the grooves on chewing surfaces to prevent decay. It is well studied in permanent teeth, but evidence for baby teeth is thin. Cochrane checked whether sealants prevent decay on baby molars. It included 9 studies with 1,120 children aged 18 months to eight years.

### What was found
Different sealants were compared: resin-based, fluoride-releasing, glass ionomer and composite, with each other and with no sealant. The studies were usually small with few cases of decay, and many had shortcomings in analysis and reporting.

### What it means for you
Certainty was low or very low. An important gap: adverse events were hardly reported. Larger, more careful trials are needed. Whether your child's baby teeth should be sealed is for the dentist to decide from decay risk.

Plain-language retelling of a published paper. Original:
- Ramamurthy P, Rath A, Sidhu P, Fernandes B, Nettem S, Fee PA, et al.. Sealants for preventing dental caries in primary teeth. Cochrane Database Syst Rev. 2022. https://doi.org/10.1002/14651858.CD012981.pub2 https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/35146744/

## Gum treatment and diabetes
URL: https://saysmiledent.github.io/SaySmile/en/articles/gum-treatment-and-diabetes/
Published: 2026-11-01

Cochrane: treating periodontitis improves blood sugar control in people with diabetes by a clinically meaningful amount compared with no treatment.

- Cochrane 2022: 35 studies, 3,249 participants, mostly type 2 diabetes.
- Treating gum disease (cleaning below the gum line) improves blood sugar control by a clinically meaningful amount.
- Moderate-certainty evidence; follow-up was 3 to 12 months.

### What was studied
Diabetes and gum disease are linked both ways: gum inflammation can make blood sugar harder to control, and diabetes raises the risk of gum problems. Cochrane checked whether treating periodontitis helps people with diabetes control their blood sugar.

### What was found
The 2022 update included 35 studies and 3,249 participants. Nearly all studied type 2 diabetes, with follow-up from 3 to 12 months. Only two studies were at low risk of bias, but the update doubled the number of studies and changed the conclusion.

### What it means for you
There is now moderate-certainty evidence that periodontal treatment with subgingival instrumentation improves blood sugar control in people with periodontitis and diabetes by a clinically significant amount compared with no treatment or usual care. The authors think further trials are unlikely to change this overall conclusion. If you have diabetes, do not put off a gum check.

Plain-language retelling of a published paper. Original:
- Simpson TC, Clarkson JE, Worthington HV, MacDonald L, Weldon JC, Needleman I, et al.. Treatment of periodontitis for glycaemic control in people with diabetes mellitus. Cochrane Database Syst Rev. 2022. https://doi.org/10.1002/14651858.CD004714.pub4 https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/35420698/

## Dental anxiety in adults
URL: https://saysmiledent.github.io/SaySmile/en/articles/dental-anxiety-in-adults/
Published: 2026-11-01

Relaxation, distraction and hypnosis can ease anxiety. Drug options such as nitrous oxide or sedation exist but carry risks.

- Dental anxiety is common and leads people to avoid care.
- Relaxation, guided imagery, distraction, hypnosis, acupuncture and desensitisation all help.
- Drug options (nitrous oxide, sedation) exist, but carry risks and contraindications.

### What was studied
Anxiety can appear before, during or after treatment, with a faster heartbeat, higher blood pressure and quicker breathing. Strong distress leads people to miss appointments and put off treatment, which harms both teeth and general health. The authors systematically reviewed ways to manage anxiety in adult patients in the dental clinic.

### What was found
Psychological methods have nil or negligible side effects: muscle relaxation, guided imagery, biofeedback, hypnosis, acupuncture, distraction and desensitisation. Drug options include nitrous oxide and intravenous or oral sedation. These can have side effects, risks and contraindications, and they raise the cost and lower the availability of care.

### What it means for you
If you are afraid, tell your dentist ahead of time: the method depends on your level of anxiety and the situation. Do not postpone treatment because of fear; it only makes it harder later.

Plain-language retelling of a published paper. Original:
- Hoffmann B, Erwood K, Ncomanzi S, Fischer V, O'Brien D, Lee A. Management strategies for adult patients with dental anxiety in the dental clinic: a systematic review. Aust Dent J. 2022. https://doi.org/10.1111/adj.12926 https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/35735746/

## Chlorhexidine mouthwash with braces
URL: https://saysmiledent.github.io/SaySmile/en/articles/chlorhexidine-mouthwash-with-braces/
Published: 2026-11-01

A meta-analysis of 14 studies (602 patients): chlorhexidine cuts plaque and gum inflammation during braces, but other mouthwashes were about as effective.

- A meta-analysis of 14 studies with 602 patients aged 11 to 35.
- Chlorhexidine reduced plaque and gum inflammation during braces.
- Some other mouthwashes were about as effective.

### What was studied
Braces make cleaning harder, and the gums often become inflamed. The authors gathered data on chlorhexidine mouthwash during treatment with fixed appliances. They searched up to December 2021 and included only randomised trials.

### What was found
Fourteen studies and 602 patients aged 11 to 35 were included. The solutions were 0.06%, 0.12% or 0.2% chlorhexidine against a placebo or other mouthwashes. Treatment lasted from one day to almost five months. Chlorhexidine reduced plaque and gum inflammation during orthodontic treatment, yet some of the comparison rinses were deemed equally effective. At 3 to 4 weeks there was no significant difference in the gingival index between chlorhexidine and rinses with propolis, probiotics or herbs.

### What it means for you
The authors conclude that chlorhexidine successfully controls gum inflammation and bleeding during braces compared with no treatment, but is equally effective as other mouthrinses. Which rinse to use and for how long is best asked of your dentist.

Plain-language retelling of a published paper. Original:
- Karamani I, Kalimeri E, Seremidi K, Gkourtsogianni S, Kloukos D. Chlorhexidine Mouthwash for Gingivitis Control in Orthodontic Patients﻿: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis. Oral Health Prev Dent. 2022. https://doi.org/10.3290/j.ohpd.b3170043 https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/35762364/

## Dry socket after extraction
URL: https://saysmiledent.github.io/SaySmile/en/articles/dry-socket-after-extraction/
Published: 2026-11-01

Cochrane: chlorhexidine rinse or gel in the socket probably reduces the risk of dry socket; evidence for 21 other measures is insufficient.

- Cochrane: 49 trials, 6,771 participants, on dry socket after a tooth extraction.
- Chlorhexidine rinse (0.12% or 0.2%) and 0.2% gel in the socket probably reduce the risk (moderate-certainty evidence).
- For 21 other preventive measures and for treatment, evidence is insufficient.

### What was studied
Dry socket is a complication of extraction, more often involving lower molars. Severe pain develops 2 to 3 days later, sometimes with bad breath, and the socket may be partly or totally without a blood clot. Cochrane gathered 49 trials with 6,771 participants: 39 on prevention and 10 on treatment. Only three trials were at low risk of bias.

### What was found
Rinsing with chlorhexidine before extraction and 24 hours after substantially reduced the risk of dry socket compared with placebo (moderate-certainty evidence). Placing 0.2% chlorhexidine gel in the socket also reduced the risk and was not better than the rinse. Dry socket occurs in 1% to 5% of routine extractions and up to 30% of surgically extracted third molars. Side effects of chlorhexidine included altered taste, tooth staining and stomatitis.

### What it means for you
For the other 21 preventive measures evidence is insufficient, and there is little evidence on treatment. After an extraction follow your dentist's advice, and tell them right away if pain gets worse on day two or three.

Plain-language retelling of a published paper. Original:
- Daly BJ, Sharif MO, Jones K, Worthington HV, Beattie A. Local interventions for the management of alveolar osteitis (dry socket). Cochrane Database Syst Rev. 2022. https://doi.org/10.1002/14651858.CD006968.pub3 https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36156769/

## Charcoal toothpaste for whitening
URL: https://saysmiledent.github.io/SaySmile/en/articles/charcoal-toothpaste-for-whitening/
Published: 2026-11-01

Activated charcoal toothpastes whiten less than other options and are more abrasive, so they are seen as less safe.

- Charcoal toothpastes whiten less than other options.
- Most studies agree they are more abrasive.
- Because of the abrasion, they are seen as less safe.

### What was studied
Adding activated charcoal to toothpaste is a fashionable "natural" way to whiten. The authors collected and analysed the studies: of 208 articles found, 11 qualified, with medium to high risk of bias.

### What was found
Whitening results varied: in some studies the products did not differ significantly, in others charcoal was not the strongest whitener. On abrasion most studies agree that charcoal toothpaste is more abrasive.

### What it means for you
The authors conclude that charcoal toothpastes whiten less than other options and, because of high abrasion, can be considered less safe. If you want whiter teeth, ask your dentist which products will not harm the enamel.

Plain-language retelling of a published paper. Original:
- Tomás DBM, Pecci-Lloret MP, Guerrero-Gironés J. Effectiveness and abrasiveness of activated charcoal as a whitening agent: A systematic review of in vitro studies. Ann Anat. 2022. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.aanat.2022.151998 https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36183933/

## How to treat tooth sensitivity successfully
URL: https://saysmiledent.github.io/SaySmile/en/articles/how-to-treat-tooth-sensitivity-successfully/
Published: 2026-11-01

A narrative review: at least one in ten people has dentin hypersensitivity, and successful treatment takes both a motivated patient and a dentist who knows the options.

- A review of dentin hypersensitivity: at least 1 in 10 people.
- The pain is short and sharp, set off by cold, sweets, touch or drying.
- Success needs both the patient and the dentist.

### What was studied
This is a narrative review. Dentin hypersensitivity affects at least one in ten people. It is a short, sharp pain in response to thermal, chemical, tactile or evaporative triggers, and it is more common in adults.

### What was found
The authors note that the pain makes eating, drinking and brushing difficult and lowers quality of life. Successful treatment needs both sides: the dentist finds the cause and chooses the method, and the patient follows the care advice.

### What it means for you
If your teeth react to cold or sweet foods, do not simply put up with it or treat it on your own. Tell your dentist exactly when the pain starts.

Plain-language retelling of a published paper. Original:
- Ramli R, Ghani N, Taib H, Mat-Baharin NH. Successful management of dentin hypersensitivity: A narrative review. Dent Med Probl. 2022. https://doi.org/10.17219/dmp/143354 https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36206495/

## Sealant or fluoride varnish for school children
URL: https://saysmiledent.github.io/SaySmile/en/articles/sealant-or-fluoride-varnish-for-school-children/
Published: 2026-11-01

After two years, sealants and fluoride varnish prevented decay about equally. The authors point out that varnish is cheaper and easier to apply.

- Sealants and fluoride varnish prevented decay on first permanent molars about equally.
- The comparison pooled 4 studies, 1,249 children and two years of follow-up.
- The authors point out that varnish is cheaper and easier to apply.

### What was studied
A sealant covers the grooves on a chewing surface, while varnish is painted on as a thin layer. Both protect against decay, but it was unclear which is better. The authors gathered randomised trials in school children and compared the two on first permanent molars.

### What was found
Four studies with 1,249 children were included. After 24 months there was no statistically significant difference in new decayed teeth or surfaces. Results varied quite a lot between the studies.

### What it means for you
For parents this means both measures work, and the choice may depend on the tooth, age and what is available. The authors stress a practical plus for varnish: it is more affordable and easier to apply. What suits your child is for your dentist to decide at a check-up.

Plain-language retelling of a published paper. Original:
- Rashed T, Alkhalefa N, Adam A, AlKheraif A. Pit and Fissure Sealant versus Fluoride Varnish for the Prevention of Dental Caries in School Children: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis. Int J Clin Pract. 2022. https://doi.org/10.1155/2022/8635254 https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36263239/

## Braces or aligners and gum health
URL: https://saysmiledent.github.io/SaySmile/en/articles/braces-or-aligners-and-gum-health/
Published: 2026-11-01

The evidence does not prove aligners are always better for gums. Hygiene instruction and motivation matter more than the type of appliance.

- Gum health with braces and with aligners was compared across 8 studies.
- Only the plaque index was better with aligners.
- Hygiene, motivation and professional follow-up may matter more than the type of appliance.

### What was studied
The authors asked whether the type of appliance changes oral hygiene and gum health. They searched PubMed, PMC and the Cochrane Library for 2005 to 2020 and ended up with 8 studies: 204 patients with aligners and 294 with multibracket appliances.

### What was found
They compared plaque index, pocket depth, gingival index and bleeding on probing. Only the plaque index showed a significant difference, and overall gum health was better with aligners. But the studies differed in age, severity of malocclusion and timing, and hygiene instruction and professional follow-up were not the same.

### What it means for you
The authors are cautious: more studies are needed before saying aligners are always better for the gums. Hygiene, patient motivation and professional support may count for more than the type of appliance.

Plain-language retelling of a published paper. Original:
- Partouche AJD, Castro F, Baptista AS, Costa LG, Fernandes JCH, Fernandes GVO. Effects of Multibracket Orthodontic Treatment versus Clear Aligners on Periodontal Health: An Integrative Review. Dent J (Basel). 2022. https://doi.org/10.3390/dj10100177 https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36285987/

## Root canal in one visit or several
URL: https://saysmiledent.github.io/SaySmile/en/articles/root-canal-in-one-visit-or-several/
Published: 2026-11-01

Cochrane found no difference in outcomes. Pain within the first week was reported more often after single-visit treatment (moderate certainty).

- Cochrane: 47 studies, 5,805 participants, root canal in one visit or several.
- No difference in outcomes, but more people reported pain within a week after a single visit.
- Neither approach prevents pain and complications over 12 months.

### What was studied
Root canal treatment is done when the pulp is inflamed or dead because of decay, a crack or an injury. It can be finished in one visit or spread over several. Cochrane compared the two in 47 studies with 5,805 participants and 5,693 teeth. Only 10 studies were at low risk of bias.

### What was found
No difference was found in radiological failure, the signs that the treatment has not worked (moderate-certainty evidence). Pain up to 72 hours, swelling or flare-ups and use of painkillers also did not differ. But pain within one week was reported more often after single-visit treatment (moderate-certainty evidence). Unlike the last version of the review, no difference in painkiller use was found.

### What it means for you
As before, there is no evidence that one approach is more effective than the other. Neither prevents pain and other complications in the 12 months after treatment. How many visits you need is for your dentist to decide from the condition of the tooth.

Plain-language retelling of a published paper. Original:
- Mergoni G, Ganim M, Lodi G, Figini L, Gagliani M, Manfredi M. Single versus multiple visits for endodontic treatment of permanent teeth. Cochrane Database Syst Rev. 2022. https://doi.org/10.1002/14651858.CD005296.pub4 https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36512807/

## Antibiotics before a tooth extraction
URL: https://saysmiledent.github.io/SaySmile/en/articles/antibiotics-before-a-tooth-extraction/
Published: 2026-11-01

Cochrane: whether to give antibiotics before an extraction should be decided per patient, by condition and infection risk. People with weak immunity need an individual plan with their doctor.

- Cochrane: 23 trials (about 3,200 participants) of antibiotics versus placebo around tooth extraction.
- After wisdom tooth removal, antibiotics may lower the risk of infection and dry socket (low-certainty evidence).
- The decision should be individual; immunocompromised patients need a tailored approach.

### What was studied
Teeth are most often extracted because of decay and gum infection. Systemic antibiotics are sometimes prescribed to prevent complications. Cochrane gathered 23 trials comparing antibiotics with placebo, with about 3,206 participants. Nearly all (21 of 23) involved healthy people having impacted wisdom teeth removed, and none looked at immunocompromised patients.

### What was found
Low-certainty evidence suggests antibiotics may cut the risk of infection after wisdom tooth removal by about 66%: about 19 healthy people need treatment to prevent one infection. They may reduce the risk of dry socket by 34%. Side effects were mild and transient, but the evidence on them is very uncertain. No clear evidence showed that timing (before, after or both) mattered.

### What it means for you
Because bacterial resistance to antibiotics is rising, the authors advise dentists to decide for each patient whether antibiotics are needed, based on their health and infection risk. Do not take them "just in case" without a prescription.

Plain-language retelling of a published paper. Original:
- Lodi G, Azzi L, Varoni EM, Pentenero M, Del Fabbro M, Carrassi A, et al.. Antibiotics to prevent complications following tooth extractions. Cochrane Database Syst Rev. 2021. https://doi.org/10.1002/14651858.CD003811.pub3 https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/33624847/

## Why teeth are removed
URL: https://saysmiledent.github.io/SaySmile/en/articles/why-teeth-are-removed/
Published: 2026-11-01

A systematic review: teeth are most often removed because of decay (36-55% of cases) and gum disease (25-38%).

- A systematic review of 3 studies covering 4,396 tooth extractions.
- The main reason for extraction was caries (36.0 to 55.3%).
- Gum disease came second (24.8 to 38.1%).

### What was studied
Why are teeth removed? The authors gathered data on the reasons for tooth extraction in adults. The review included 3 studies that analysed 4,396 extractions.

### What was found
Caries was the reason in 36.0 to 55.3% of cases and periodontal disease in 24.8 to 38.1%. Periapical disease accounted for 7.3 to 19.1%, orthodontic reasons for 2.5 to 7.2%, trauma for 0.8 to 4.4%, other reasons for 4.5 to 9.2% and the patient's own request for 3.6 to 5.9%.

### What it means for you
The conclusion: most extractions are linked to decay and gum disease, so a large share could be prevented by good care and early treatment.

Plain-language retelling of a published paper. Original:
- Broers DLM, Dubois L, de Lange J, Su N, de Jongh A. Reasons for Tooth Removal in Adults: A Systematic Review. Int Dent J. 2021. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.identj.2021.01.011 https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/33648772/

## Rubber dam for fillings
URL: https://saysmiledent.github.io/SaySmile/en/articles/rubber-dam-for-fillings/
Published: 2026-11-01

A rubber dam may lower the failure rate of fillings after six months compared with cotton rolls. At other time points the evidence is uncertain.

- A rubber dam may lower the failure rate of fillings after six months compared with cotton rolls.
- At other time points the evidence is very uncertain.
- All six studies had a high risk of bias; better research is needed.

### What was studied
A rubber dam is a thin rubber sheet that keeps a tooth isolated from saliva during treatment. Cochrane compared it with ordinary cotton rolls for fillings. It found six studies from 2010 to 2015 with 1,342 participants, four of which entered the analysis.

### What was found
In two studies with 192 participants, the rubber dam may increase the survival of composite fillings at the neck of the tooth. After six months fewer fillings failed with a rubber dam than with cotton rolls (low certainty). At other time points the evidence is very uncertain.

### What it means for you
All studies had a high risk of bias, so the authors ask for new high-quality work on different types of fillings. A rubber dam also helps the dentist work on a dry tooth, which is why many dentists use it when they can.

Plain-language retelling of a published paper. Original:
- Miao C, Yang X, Wong MC, Zou J, Zhou X, Li C, et al.. Rubber dam isolation for restorative treatment in dental patients. Cochrane Database Syst Rev. 2021. https://doi.org/10.1002/14651858.CD009858.pub3 https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/33998662/

## Treating cavities: which approach
URL: https://saysmiledent.github.io/SaySmile/en/articles/treating-cavities-which-approach/
Published: 2026-11-01

Cochrane compared ways of treating cavitated decay across 27 studies. For most comparisons our confidence in the results is low.

- Cochrane compared ways of treating cavitated decay across 27 studies.
- Compared with conventional care, the Hall Technique and selective removal failed less in baby teeth, and selective and stepwise removal in permanent teeth.
- For most comparisons certainty is low or very low.

### What was studied
When a tooth already has a cavity, a dentist can remove all the decay or leave part of the affected tissue. Cochrane gathered 27 studies with 3,350 participants and 4,195 teeth from 11 countries. Most involved children and teenagers, and baby and permanent teeth were both studied.

### What was found
Conventional treatment was compared with less invasive ones: selective removal (SE), stepwise removal (SW), the Hall Technique (HT) and others. Compared with conventional treatment there were fewer failures with HT and SE in baby teeth, and with SE and SW in permanent teeth.

### What it means for you
Most studies had a high risk of bias and small samples, so the authors rated confidence in most comparisons as low or very low. The practical message: gentle approaches look promising, but the choice is made by your dentist together with you.

Plain-language retelling of a published paper. Original:
- Schwendicke F, Walsh T, Lamont T, Al-Yaseen W, Bjørndal L, Clarkson JE, et al.. Interventions for treating cavitated or dentine carious lesions. Cochrane Database Syst Rev. 2021. https://doi.org/10.1002/14651858.CD013039.pub2 https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/34280957/

## Why teeth become sensitive
URL: https://saysmiledent.github.io/SaySmile/en/articles/why-teeth-become-sensitive/
Published: 2026-11-01

A review: five explanations have been proposed for the pain of dentin sensitivity. They do not exclude each other, and understanding them may lead to new treatments.

- A review of why exposed dentin hurts.
- Five mechanisms are proposed, and they are not mutually exclusive.
- A clearer understanding may lead to new drugs.

### What was studied
Why does a tooth hurt from cold when it has no hole? The authors gathered the theories about pain from exposed dentin. Dentin is full of tiny channels leading to the nerve of the tooth.

### What was found
Five mechanisms are proposed: hydrodynamic (fluid moving in the tubules), direct innervation of the tubules, neuroplasticity and sensitisation, odontoblasts acting as sensory receptors, and algoneurons. These mechanisms are not mutually exclusive and may act together.

### What it means for you
The authors believe a clear understanding of the mechanisms may help develop new drugs. For now the dentist chooses treatment based on the cause and your situation.

Plain-language retelling of a published paper. Original:
- Aminoshariae A, Kulild JC. Current Concepts of Dentinal Hypersensitivity. J Endod. 2021. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.joen.2021.07.011 https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/34302871/

## Fillings: composite or amalgam
URL: https://saysmiledent.github.io/SaySmile/en/articles/fillings-composite-or-amalgam/
Published: 2026-11-01

Cochrane: in 8 studies composite fillings in permanent back teeth failed more often and had more secondary decay (low certainty); no important harms to health were found.

- Cochrane 2021: 8 trials, mostly in children; 921 children in the main analysis.
- Composite fillings failed almost twice as often as amalgam and had more secondary decay.
- Certainty is low; all studies had a high risk of bias.

### What was studied
Composite (tooth-coloured) and amalgam (silver) fillings are used to treat decay. Cochrane compared them mainly in children's baby and permanent teeth. It included 8 randomised trials, with 921 children in the main analysis.

### What was found
Composite restorations had almost double the risk of failure (RR 1.89) and a higher risk of secondary decay (RR 2.14). The risk of fracture was not higher. Certainty was low. Urinary mercury was higher with amalgam but below toxic levels. No consistent clinically important harms were found (very low certainty). All studies had a high risk of bias.

### What it means for you
The authors conclude the evidence is of low certainty. The choice of material depends on the tooth, its position and the child, and the dentist makes it.

Plain-language retelling of a published paper. Original:
- Worthington HV, Khangura S, Seal K, Mierzwinski-Urban M, Veitz-Keenan A, Sahrmann P, et al.. Direct composite resin fillings versus amalgam fillings for permanent posterior teeth. Cochrane Database Syst Rev. 2021. https://doi.org/10.1002/14651858.CD005620.pub3 https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/34387873/

## Gentle treatment of decay in baby teeth
URL: https://saysmiledent.github.io/SaySmile/en/articles/gentle-treatment-of-decay-in-baby-teeth/
Published: 2026-11-01

An umbrella review of minimal intervention methods (SDF, Hall Technique, selective removal) in baby teeth. They did better than no treatment and compared well with conventional fillings.

- Gentle treatments for decay in baby teeth effectively halt its progress.
- They include 38% SDF, the Hall Technique, selective removal of decay and ART.
- The authors urge treating them as a mainstream option, not a compromise.

### What was studied
Not every child tolerates the drill well, and not every tooth needs full cleaning-out. This is an "umbrella review": the authors gathered 18 systematic reviews from 2006 to 2020 on minimally invasive treatment of dentine decay in baby teeth.

### What was found
Eight reviews covered 38% silver diamine fluoride, one the Hall Technique, one selective removal of decayed tissue and eight atraumatic restorative treatment (ART). For single-surface cavities these methods appear effective at arresting decay compared with no treatment or conventional fillings.

### What it means for you
The authors urge that such methods be seen as mainstream options, not as a compromise when conventional care is not possible because of cooperation or cost. The right method for your child is for the dentist to choose.

Plain-language retelling of a published paper. Original:
- BaniHani A, Santamaría RM, Hu S, Maden M, Albadri S. Minimal intervention dentistry for managing carious lesions into dentine in primary teeth: an umbrella review. Eur Arch Paediatr Dent. 2021. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40368-021-00675-6 https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/34784027/

## Posterior crossbite
URL: https://saysmiledent.github.io/SaySmile/en/articles/posterior-crossbite/
Published: 2026-11-01

Cochrane: in children with a posterior crossbite the quad-helix worked better than expansion plates. For other comparisons the evidence was insufficient.

- Cochrane found 31 studies on posterior crossbite in children and teenagers (about 1,410 participants).
- At ages 7 to 11, quad-helix and expansion plates beat observation; quad-helix works better than plates.
- At ages 12 to 16, Hyrax and Haas performed alike.

### What was studied
In a posterior crossbite the top back teeth bite inside the bottom ones. It affects about 4% of children and adolescents in Europe and 17% in America. Cochrane compared treatments: 31 studies with about 1,410 participants were included.

### What was found
For children aged 7 to 11, quad-helix corrected the bite far better than observation alone (high-certainty evidence) and widened the distance between the molars. Expansion plates also helped, but quad-helix corrected the crossbite more effectively and in less time. For teenagers aged 12 to 16, Hyrax and Haas did not differ in correcting the crossbite (moderate-certainty evidence).

### What it means for you
For the remaining comparisons the evidence is insufficient for firm conclusions. Which appliance a child needs and when to start is for the orthodontist to decide after an examination.

Plain-language retelling of a published paper. Original:
- Ugolini A, Agostino P, Silvestrini-Biavati A, Harrison JE, Batista KB. Orthodontic treatment for posterior crossbites. Cochrane Database Syst Rev. 2021. https://doi.org/10.1002/14651858.CD000979.pub3 https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/34951927/

## Cleaning below the gum line for gum disease
URL: https://saysmiledent.github.io/SaySmile/en/articles/cleaning-below-the-gum-line-for-gum-disease/
Published: 2026-11-01

A systematic review: cleaning the pockets under the gums cut pocket depth by about 1.4 mm at 6 to 8 months, and the type of instrument or the order of visits made no major difference.

- A systematic review of randomised trials on cleaning below the gum line.
- Pocket depth fell by about 1.4 mm at 6 to 8 months and about 74% of pockets closed.
- Hand and ultrasonic instruments, and how the visits are arranged, made no major difference.

### What was studied
Gum disease treatment starts with cleaning the roots below the gums: the dentist removes plaque and tartar from the pockets. The authors checked how well this works, whether hand and ultrasonic instruments differ, and whether it is better to work area by area or the whole mouth in a short time. They searched databases up to March 2019.

### What was found
Almost no trials compared it with cleaning above the gum line only, so before-and-after data from 9 studies were used. Pocket depth fell by 1.4 mm on average at 6 to 8 months, and about 74% of pockets closed. Six trials compared hand with sonic or ultrasonic instruments and found no difference. Thirteen trials compared quadrant-by-quadrant with full-mouth cleaning and again found none. Five studies reported patient-reported outcomes, with no differences.

### What it means for you
The authors conclude that mechanical cleaning below the gum line is an efficacious way to control infection in people with periodontitis, whatever the instrument or the mode of delivery. So coming for treatment on time matters more than the choice of instrument.

Plain-language retelling of a published paper. Original:
- Suvan J, Leira Y, Moreno Sancho FM, Graziani F, Derks J, Tomasi C. Subgingival instrumentation for treatment of periodontitis. A systematic review. J Clin Periodontol. 2020. https://doi.org/10.1111/jcpe.13245 https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/31889320/

## Antibiotic pills in gum treatment
URL: https://saysmiledent.github.io/SaySmile/en/articles/antibiotic-pills-in-gum-treatment/
Published: 2026-11-01

A meta-analysis of 28 studies: antibiotics taken alongside pocket cleaning add a small benefit, but side effects were reported more often.

- A meta-analysis of 28 studies (34 articles) with follow-up of at least 6 months.
- Antibiotics added to pocket cleaning gave a small extra benefit.
- Amoxicillin with metronidazole worked best; side effects were reported more often.

### What was studied
In gum disease the dentist cleans the pockets under the gums and sometimes adds antibiotic tablets. The authors checked whether this gives extra benefit compared with cleaning plus a placebo. The analysis included 28 studies (34 articles) with follow-up of at least 6 months.

### What was found
Antibiotics gave a statistically significant benefit for pocket depth, about 0.45 mm in both short and long term. Attachment level, bleeding, pocket closure and the share of residual pockets also improved. The best results came from amoxicillin plus metronidazole, followed by metronidazole alone and azithromycin.

### What it means for you
Adverse events were reported more often in the antibiotic groups. The authors conclude there is a benefit, but the decision is the dentist's: antibiotics are not for everyone and should not be taken on your own.

Plain-language retelling of a published paper. Original:
- Teughels W, Feres M, Oud V, Martín C, Matesanz P, Herrera D. Adjunctive effect of systemic antimicrobials in periodontitis therapy: A systematic review and meta-analysis. J Clin Periodontol. 2020. https://doi.org/10.1111/jcpe.13264 https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/31994207/

## Dentin sensitivity: causes and care
URL: https://saysmiledent.github.io/SaySmile/en/articles/dentin-sensitivity-causes-and-care/
Published: 2026-11-01

An overview of causes, diagnosis and treatment of tooth sensitivity. Desensitising agents close the tubules, but the long-term outcome is uncertain.

- Dentin hypersensitivity is one of the most common complaints in dental clinics.
- There are no universally accepted guidelines for diagnosis or choosing treatment.
- Desensitising agents close the tubules, but the long-term outcome is uncertain.

### What was studied
Tooth sensitivity is one of the most common complaints in dental clinics, yet there are no universally accepted guidelines for differential diagnosis or for choosing reliable treatment. The mechanisms behind the pain are unclear. The most widely accepted explanation is the hydrodynamic theory: fluid movement within exposed dentinal tubules causes the pain.

### What was found
Several dental conditions have symptoms that mimic sensitivity at different stages, so diagnosis and treatment are often confusing, especially for inexperienced practitioners. The authors review risk factors for the development and chronicity of sensitivity and summarise principles of diagnosis and management.

### What it means for you
Desensitisation remains the first choice, and most agents reduce symptoms by occluding open dentinal tubules. But the long-term outcome of such treatment is uncertain. The authors expect that better understanding of the pain mechanisms will bring more effective therapies. If your teeth hurt with cold or sweet things, see a dentist to rule out other causes.

Plain-language retelling of a published paper. Original:
- Liu XX, Tenenbaum HC, Wilder RS, Quock R, Hewlett ER, Ren YF. Pathogenesis, diagnosis and management of dentin hypersensitivity: an evidence-based overview for dental practitioners. BMC Oral Health. 2020. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12903-020-01199-z https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32762733/

## Dentin decay in baby teeth: how to intervene
URL: https://saysmiledent.github.io/SaySmile/en/articles/dentin-decay-in-baby-teeth-how-to-intervene/
Published: 2026-11-01

Less invasive approaches (selective or no decay removal) look better than complete removal. Preformed crowns are supported for multi-surface molars.

- Less invasive approaches (selective or no removal of decay) look better than removing it completely.
- Preformed metal crowns did best for multi-surface lesions in baby teeth.
- SDF arrested decay significantly better than other methods.

### What was studied
This paper was prepared for an expert consensus (ORCA/EFCD). The authors gathered evidence on how best to intervene in dentine decay of baby teeth and which materials to use. They looked at 2 systematic reviews and 5 randomised trials on treatment success, and 10 reviews and 1 trial on non-restorative options, all with at least 12 months of follow-up.

### What was found
In deep lesions, selective removal reduced pulp exposure, but its benefit over complete removal for symptoms or filling success was not confirmed. For multi-surface lesions, preformed metal crowns had higher success rates than amalgam, composite and glass ionomer. Among non-restorative options, silver diamine fluoride arrested decay significantly better than other treatments.

### What it means for you
The authors note much variation between studies, but the trends agreed: in a child whose tooth is vital and painless, less invasive approaches look better than complete decay removal. What suits a child is for the dentist to decide.

Plain-language retelling of a published paper. Original:
- Santamaría RM, Abudrya MH, Gül G, Mourad MS, Gomez GF, Zandona AGF. How to Intervene in the Caries Process: Dentin Caries in Primary Teeth. Caries Res. 2020. https://doi.org/10.1159/000508899 https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32854105/

## How common is tooth sensitivity
URL: https://saysmiledent.github.io/SaySmile/en/articles/how-common-is-tooth-sensitivity/
Published: 2026-11-01

A meta-analysis of 65 papers: the best estimate of dentin hypersensitivity is 11.5%, but figures vary widely between studies, from 1.3% to 92.1%.

- A systematic review of 65 papers and 77 studies.
- Estimates of dentin hypersensitivity varied widely, from 1.3% to 92.1%.
- The best estimate was about 11.5%; it was higher in younger adults and in specialty-practice patients.

### What was studied
Dentin hypersensitivity is a short, sharp pain in a tooth from cold, sweet foods or touch. The authors asked how common it is worldwide. They searched several databases and included 65 publications covering 77 studies.

### What was found
Estimates varied a lot, from 1.3% to 92.1%, because the studies defined the problem differently and chose people differently. The best estimate from pooled data was 11.5%, with an average of 33.5%. It was higher among patients of specialty practices and among younger adults.

### What it means for you
The authors conclude that prevalence varies, but the problem is far from rare. If your teeth react sharply to cold or sweet foods, tell your dentist. The cause can be found and a suitable treatment chosen.

Plain-language retelling of a published paper. Original:
- Favaro Zeola L, Soares PV, Cunha-Cruz J. Prevalence of dentin hypersensitivity: Systematic review and meta-analysis. J Dent. 2019. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jdent.2018.12.015 https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30639724/

## Fluoride toothpaste: which strength?
URL: https://saysmiledent.github.io/SaySmile/en/articles/fluoride-toothpaste-which-strength/
Published: 2026-11-01

Fluoride toothpaste prevents decay in children. For many strength comparisons the evidence is uncertain, and for young children the choice must be weighed against the risk of fluorosis.

- Fluoride toothpaste prevents decay in children compared with toothpaste without fluoride.
- More fluoride often means more protection, but for many comparisons the evidence is still thin.
- For young children the choice should be weighed against the risk of fluorosis (marks on enamel).

### What was studied
This is a Cochrane review of 96 studies published between 1955 and 2014. Children and teenagers used toothpaste with different amounts of fluoride, and the studies counted how many new teeth and tooth surfaces developed decay.

### What was found
Fluoride toothpaste protects against decay better than toothpaste without it. For different strengths the picture is less clear: in children and teenagers more fluoride tended to mean more protection, but in many comparisons the result is uncertain and new studies could change it.

### What it means for you
For small children, care is needed. The authors remind readers that the choice of strength should be balanced against the risk of fluorosis. Which toothpaste and how much to use for a child is worth asking your dentist.

Plain-language retelling of a published paper. Original:
- Walsh T, Worthington HV, Glenny AM, Marinho VC, Jeroncic A. Fluoride toothpastes of different concentrations for preventing dental caries. Cochrane Database Syst Rev. 2019. https://doi.org/10.1002/14651858.CD007868.pub3 https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30829399/

## Floss and interdental brushes
URL: https://saysmiledent.github.io/SaySmile/en/articles/floss-and-interdental-brushes/
Published: 2026-11-01

Interdental brushes may reduce gum inflammation more than floss. The evidence is low in certainty and the effect may be small.

- Floss or interdental brushes added to brushing may reduce gum inflammation and plaque more than brushing alone.
- Interdental brushes may work better than floss.
- Evidence is low in certainty and the effect may be small in clinical terms.

### What was studied
A toothbrush does not reach well between teeth. Cochrane checked whether floss, interdental brushes, oral irrigators and cleaning sticks help when used on top of toothbrushing, and compared these tools with each other.

### What was found
Floss or interdental brushes added to brushing may reduce gum inflammation and plaque more than brushing alone. Interdental brushes may do better than floss. For irrigators and cleaning sticks, evidence is limited and inconsistent.

### What it means for you
Most results were measured over a short time in people with mild inflammation, and certainty is low. The authors write that the effect may not be clinically important. Which tool suits you is best asked of your dentist or hygienist.

Plain-language retelling of a published paper. Original:
- Worthington HV, MacDonald L, Poklepovic Pericic T, Sambunjak D, Johnson TM, Imai P, et al.. Home use of interdental cleaning devices, in addition to toothbrushing, for preventing and controlling periodontal diseases and dental caries. Cochrane Database Syst Rev. 2019. https://doi.org/10.1002/14651858.CD012018.pub2 https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30968949/

## Oral care for people with intellectual disabilities
URL: https://saysmiledent.github.io/SaySmile/en/articles/oral-care-for-people-with-intellectual-disabilities/
Published: 2026-11-01

Evidence on oral hygiene methods for people with intellectual disabilities is limited. Care should follow professional expertise and the needs of the person and their carers.

- For people with intellectual disabilities, evidence on the best oral hygiene methods is limited.
- Electric and manual brushes reduced gum inflammation equally in the medium term (moderate certainty).
- Care should rest on professional expertise and the needs of the person and their carers.

### What was studied
Plaque causes decay and gum disease, and brushing can be hard for people with intellectual disabilities. Cochrane gathered 34 studies, 19 randomised and 15 non-randomised, with 1,795 adults and children and 354 carers.

### What was found
They tested special manual brushes, electric brushes, hygiene training, scheduled visits with supervised brushing, discussion of plaque photos, different brushing frequency, plaque-disclosing agents and individual care plans. Studies were small, with high or unclear risk of bias. Only one finding has moderate certainty: electric and manual brushes were equally good at reducing gum inflammation in the medium term.

### What it means for you
Some measures show benefit, but their clinical importance is unclear and data are scarce. Until then the authors advise basing care on professional expertise and on the needs and preferences of the person and their carers. A dentist can build the best plan for your relative together with you.

Plain-language retelling of a published paper. Original:
- Waldron C, Nunn J, Mac Giolla Phadraig C, Comiskey C, Guerin S, van Harten MT, et al.. Oral hygiene interventions for people with intellectual disabilities. Cochrane Database Syst Rev. 2019. https://doi.org/10.1002/14651858.CD012628.pub2 https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/31149734/

## Mother programmes run by non-dental staff
URL: https://saysmiledent.github.io/SaySmile/en/articles/mother-programmes-run-by-non-dental-staff/
Published: 2026-11-01

Oral health programmes for expectant and new mothers delivered by non-dental staff may help children, though the evidence is still weak.

- Programmes for mothers delivered by non-dental staff (such as midwives and nurses) may improve children's dental health.
- The benefit lasted when programmes were combined with referral reminders.
- Evidence is still weak: most of the 9 studies were of low quality.

### What was studied
Expectant and new mothers meet midwives, nurses and paediatric staff more often than dentists. The authors checked whether oral health programmes run by such staff help. They found 9 studies in expectant mothers or mothers of infants up to 24 months, with outcomes measured in children under 5.

### What was found
The programmes were mainly oral health education (8 studies), dental referrals (3) and oral health assessments (1). Six studies were of low methodological quality. Programmes in the antenatal or postnatal periods meaningfully improved children's dental condition and mothers' oral health habits, and the improvement was sustained when a suite of interventions was used with referral reminders.

### What it means for you
The authors conclude that non-dental professionals can support maternal oral health through education, risk assessment and referrals, though the evidence is weak. Higher-quality studies are needed to show when such programmes are best delivered.

Plain-language retelling of a published paper. Original:
- George A, Sousa MS, Kong AC, Blinkhorn A, Patterson Norrie T, Foster J, et al.. Effectiveness of preventive dental programs offered to mothers by non-dental professionals to control early childhood dental caries: a review. BMC Oral Health. 2019. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12903-019-0862-x https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/31375106/

## Halitosis: how common and how treated
URL: https://saysmiledent.github.io/SaySmile/en/articles/halitosis-how-common-and-how-treated/
Published: 2026-11-01

A literature review of how common bad breath is, where it comes from, and how it is measured and treated.

- Bad breath has many sources and affects quality of life.
- Clinicians need to know how common it is, where it comes from and what the risk factors are.
- The authors reviewed how it is measured and treated.

### What was studied
Halitosis is an offensive breath odour. It has many sources and affects social interaction and quality of life. To diagnose and treat it properly, health professionals need to understand its causes and risk factors.

### What was found
The authors reviewed the literature and covered six topics: how common halitosis is, how it is classified, risk factors, sources, measurement and treatment.

### What it means for you
For an ordinary reader the main point is that bad breath is a common and manageable problem, not something to be ashamed of. If it worries you, see a clinician: the source is found first, then the treatment is chosen.

Plain-language retelling of a published paper. Original:
- Wu J, Cannon RD, Ji P, Farella M, Mei L. Halitosis: prevalence, risk factors, sources, measurement and treatment - a review of the literature. Aust Dent J. 2019. https://doi.org/10.1111/adj.12725 https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/31610030/

## Preventing early childhood decay through mothers
URL: https://saysmiledent.github.io/SaySmile/en/articles/preventing-early-childhood-decay-through-mothers/
Published: 2026-11-01

Cochrane (2019, 17 trials): diet and feeding advice for mothers and carers of children up to one year probably slightly lowers the risk of early childhood decay. Other measures are not well enough studied.

- Cochrane 2019: 17 trials, about 23,700 caregivers and their children.
- Diet and feeding advice for mothers and carers of children up to one year probably slightly lowers the risk of early decay.
- Other measures are not well enough studied.

### What was studied
This is the earlier version of the same Cochrane review on preventing childhood decay through pregnant women and mothers. It included 17 trials with 23,732 caregivers (mostly mothers) and their children.

### What was found
Eleven trials tested education: child diet advice, diet and feeding advice, breastfeeding support, and hygiene with diet and feeding advice. Six studied dental treatment for the mother, including chlorhexidine, iodine with fluoride and xylitol.

### What it means for you
Only one finding has moderate certainty: diet and feeding advice for pregnant women, mothers or carers of children up to one year probably slightly lowers the risk of early childhood decay. For other measures evidence is insufficient and large, high-quality trials are needed.

Plain-language retelling of a published paper. Original:
- Riggs E, Kilpatrick N, Slack-Smith L, Chadwick B, Yelland J, Muthu MS, et al.. Interventions with pregnant women, new mothers and other primary caregivers for preventing early childhood caries. Cochrane Database Syst Rev. 2019. https://doi.org/10.1002/14651858.CD012155.pub2 https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/31745970/

## Dentures: impression techniques
URL: https://saysmiledent.github.io/SaySmile/en/articles/dentures-impression-techniques/
Published: 2026-11-01

Cochrane found no clear advantage for any final-impression technique or material for complete and partial dentures. The evidence is low in quality.

- Cochrane found 9 studies on final impressions for complete and partial dentures.
- No technique or material showed a clear advantage.
- Evidence is low or very low quality; better trials are needed.

### What was studied
When teeth are missing, complete or partial removable dentures replace them. To make a well-fitting denture, the dentist takes a final impression using different techniques and materials. Cochrane checked which works best. It included 9 studies: eight with 485 participants with complete dentures and one with 72 participants with partial dentures. Six of the eight were at high risk of bias.

### What was found
The studies compared techniques, materials and combinations, for example silicone against alginate, and one-stage against two-stage impressions. In one study silicone gave better oral health-related quality of life, but overall no clear difference between approaches was found.

### What it means for you
The authors conclude there is no clear evidence that any technique or material has a substantial advantage. The evidence is limited and of low or very low quality, so results should be read with caution. The choice of method stays with your dentist.

Plain-language retelling of a published paper. Original:
- Jayaraman S, Singh BP, Ramanathan B, Pazhaniappan Pillai M, MacDonald L, Kirubakaran R. Final-impression techniques and materials for making complete and removable partial dentures. Cochrane Database Syst Rev. 2018. https://doi.org/10.1002/14651858.CD012256.pub2 https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/29617037/

## Glass ionomer or composite in baby teeth
URL: https://saysmiledent.github.io/SaySmile/en/articles/glass-ionomer-or-composite-in-baby-teeth/
Published: 2026-11-01

The two materials performed similarly in baby teeth. Glass ionomer had less secondary decay, especially with a rubber dam.

- Glass ionomer and composite performed about equally in fillings between baby molars.
- Glass ionomer had less secondary decay.
- The advantage was clearest for resin-modified glass ionomer and when a rubber dam was used.

### What was studied
Parents often ask what is best for fillings in baby teeth. The authors compared two materials: glass ionomer cement and composite resin, in Class II fillings, the ones between back teeth. They found 10 randomised trials, 9 of which went into the analysis.

### What was found
In total failures the two materials were similar. The result did not change when short follow-ups were excluded, when cements were split by type, or by the type of isolation (cotton roll or rubber dam). But glass ionomer had significantly less secondary decay, meaning decay under the filling.

### What it means for you
The advantage of glass ionomer was greater for the resin-modified type and with a rubber dam. Your dentist chooses the material by tooth, cavity size and treatment conditions, and it is worth asking about it.

Plain-language retelling of a published paper. Original:
- Dias AGA, Magno MB, Delbem ACB, Cunha RF, Maia LC, Pessan JP. Clinical performance of glass ionomer cement and composite resin in Class II restorations in primary teeth: A systematic review and meta-analysis.
